section.title: Peter's Confession
section.sectionRationale: This is the hinge of Mark's Gospel. At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, and immediately Jesus begins to teach that the Christ must suffer, be killed, and rise. Peter rebukes Him and is rebuked as Satan. Jesus then defines discipleship itself as cross-bearing: to follow Him is to deny self, lose one's life to save it, and never be ashamed of Him.
section.thesis: Jesus is indeed the Christ, but a Christ who must suffer and die and rise, and to follow this Messiah is to take up the cross, so that only the one who loses his life for Jesus and the gospel will truly save it.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the confession of Peter; the first prediction of the Passion and Peter's rebuke; the call to take up the cross; and the promise that the kingdom will come with power.

verses.text: Then Jesus and His disciples went on to the villages around Caesarea Philippi. On the way, He questioned His disciples: “Who do people say I am?”
They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, one of the prophets.”
“But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “You are the {{christos|Christ}}.”
And Jesus warned them not to tell anyone about Him.

units.label: The first prediction of the Passion
units.note: the Son of Man must suffer

verses.text: Then He began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and after three days rise again.
He spoke this message quite frankly, and Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him.
But Jesus, turning and looking at His disciples, rebuked Peter and said, “Get behind Me, Satan! For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.”

units.label: Take up your cross
units.note: whoever loses his life for My sake will save it

verses.text: Then Jesus called the crowd to Him along with His disciples, and He told them, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must {{aparneomai|deny}} himself and take up his {{stauros|cross}} and follow Me.
For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it.
What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his {{psyche|soul}}?
Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul?
If anyone is ashamed of Me and My words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when He comes in His Father’s glory with the holy angels.”

units.label: The kingdom coming with power
units.note: some will not taste death before they see it

verses.text: Then Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God arrive with power.”

christos.gloss: Anointed One, Messiah, the promised King of David's line. Peter's confession is right and pivotal, but incomplete, for he does not yet grasp that this Christ must reign through suffering and death. Jesus accepts the title and at once redefines it by the cross.

aparneomai.gloss: To deny, disown, renounce. To deny oneself is to renounce self-rule and self-interest as the centre of life, handing over the throne of one's heart to Jesus. The same verb describes Peter's later denial of Jesus, a sobering counterpoint to this call.

stauros.gloss: A cross, the Roman instrument of execution carried by the condemned to the place of death. To take up one's cross is not merely to bear hardship but to walk the road of death to self, following the crucified Messiah wherever it leads.

psyche.gloss: Life, soul, the whole self. Jesus plays on its double sense: grasping to save one's earthly life is to forfeit one's true and eternal self, while losing one's life for Him and the gospel is to save it. Nothing gained in the world can outweigh the soul.

basic.context: On the road near Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks His disciples who people say He is, and then who they say He is. Peter answers rightly: You are the Christ. But when Jesus begins to teach that the Christ must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise, Peter takes Him aside to rebuke Him, and Jesus turns and rebukes Peter as Satan, for thinking like men, not God. Then Jesus tells the crowd and disciples what following Him means: deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Him. Whoever tries to save his life will lose it; whoever loses it for Jesus and the gospel will save it. To be ashamed of Him now is to be disowned when He comes in glory. And He promises that some standing there will see the kingdom come with power.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the turning point of Mark. Up to now the question has been who Jesus is; from here the question is what kind of Christ He is, and what kind of disciples His followers must be. Peter's right confession and immediate error show that even true faith can misunderstand the way of the cross. Jesus binds His identity and His disciples' path together: the suffering Messiah calls a cross-bearing people.
basic.originalLanguages: Peter confesses Jesus as the christos, the Messiah. Jesus calls disciples to aparneomai, deny, themselves and take up the stauros, the cross. To cling to one's psyche, one's life or soul, is to lose it; to lose it for Him is to save it.
basic.typology: The suffering Son of Man fulfils the pattern of the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 and the rejected stone of the Psalms. Taking up the cross to follow the crucified King anticipates the whole shape of Christian discipleship.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Christ, but a crucified and risen Christ. He is the Son of Man who must suffer, be killed, and rise, and who will return in the Father's glory. His identity and His mission cannot be separated.
basic.god: God's way is not the way of human power and self-preservation but of the cross. To have in mind the things of God is to embrace the suffering path Jesus walks and calls His people to walk.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53 foretells the suffering servant. Psalm 118 speaks of the rejected stone. Philippians 2 traces Christ's humbling and exaltation.
basic.oneStory: The long expectation of the Messiah reaches its clarifying moment. Jesus is the Christ, but He will reign by dying and rising, not by conquering as Israel hoped. And those who follow Him must take up their own crosses. The whole Gospel now turns toward Jerusalem and the cross where the Christ will save His people by losing His life.

context.literary:
Mark sets this passage as the centre of a large frame. The first half of the Gospel moves from the baptism, where a voice from heaven names Jesus the Son, to the confession here. The second half, from 8:27 to 10:52, is held together by the word way. The scene opens on the way, verse 27, and the section ends with the healed Bartimaeus following Jesus on the way, Mark 10:52. Three times in that stretch Jesus announces His passion, 8:31, 9:31 and 10:33, and each time the announcement is followed by a failure of the disciples to understand and then by teaching on discipleship. Verses 31 to 38 are the first full cycle: prediction, misunderstanding, teaching.

Within the passage the structure turns on two questions. Who do people say I am, and who do you say I am. The first draws a list of popular guesses, the second a single confession. The structure then reverses on itself. Jesus asks about identity and Peter answers rightly, but then Jesus speaks about the Son of Man, and Peter answers wrongly. Mark shows that the same man can be right in verse 29 and Satan's mouthpiece in verse 33 within four verses.

The saying about the cross is the high point of the teaching, and it is held together by a chain of for statements in verses 35 to 38. Each for gives a reason for the one before: lose your life to save it, because what you gain is nothing against what you forfeit, because the Son of Man will be ashamed of those who are ashamed of Him. The section ends with verse 9:1, which many read as a bridge to the transfiguration six days later, Mark 9:2.

Mark also controls what the reader knows. The command to silence in verse 30 is one of his devices. The reader is told who Jesus is, but is also told that the telling must wait until it can be heard with the cross in view.
context.historical:
Caesarea Philippi lay at the foot of Mount Hermon, at one of the springs that feed the Jordan, on the northern edge of the land Israel had once held. The place had a long pagan history. A cave and spring there were associated with the Greek god Pan, and the earlier name of the town was Panias. Herod the Great had built a temple to Caesar Augustus nearby, and his son Philip refounded the town as a city and named it in honour of the emperor, adding his own name to distinguish it from the Caesarea on the coast. Mark says only that Jesus went to the villages around it, but the setting is hard to overlook: in a place that honoured an emperor who was called a son of god, a Galilean peasant is asked whether He is the Christ.

The expectations of Jesus' day were varied. The answers the disciples report in verse 28 are the popular guesses already recorded in Mark 6:14-15. John the Baptist returned from the dead, Elijah, whom Malachi said would come before the day of the LORD, Malachi 4:5, or one of the prophets. Those who spoke of the Christ, the anointed one, usually meant a son of David who would deliver Israel from her enemies. Anointed kings were a familiar figure, and Psalm 2:2 speaks of the nations rising against the LORD and His Anointed One. Nothing in the common expectation had room for a Christ who would be rejected by Israel's own leaders and killed.

The elders, chief priests and scribes that Jesus names in verse 31 are the three groups that made up the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, which will try Him in Mark 14 and 15. The prediction names His judges ahead of time.

Crucifixion was the Roman penalty for slaves and rebels. Those condemned carried the crossbeam to the place of execution, as Simon of Cyrene is made to do for Jesus in Mark 15:21. When Jesus speaks of taking up a cross to a crowd in Galilee, His hearers would have known what He meant, a condemned man walking to his death. The statement about being ashamed also has a Roman edge: crucifixion was the most shameful death, and to follow a crucified leader in public would expose a disciple to contempt.
context.canonical:
The confession draws on the Old Testament's picture of the anointed one. Kings, priests and prophets were anointed with oil, and the Psalms speak of the LORD's Anointed as the one set on the throne of Zion against the nations, Psalm 2:2 and Psalm 110:1. Isaiah's servant says that the Spirit of the Lord has anointed Him to preach good news to the poor, Isaiah 61:1. When Peter says christos, he is using the Greek word for what the Hebrew calls the Messiah, the long-awaited anointed king.

The prediction puts a second set of texts beside the first. Jesus fills the title with the Son of Man of Daniel 7:13-14, who comes with the clouds and receives everlasting dominion, and joins it to the suffering of Isaiah 53, where the servant is despised and rejected, pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, Isaiah 53:3-5. The rejection by the builders recalls Psalm 118:22, which Mark himself will have Jesus quote in Mark 12:10. What Jesus does is combine a glorious figure and a suffering figure that most of His contemporaries kept apart. Isaiah also says that the servant will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted, Isaiah 52:13, which fits the promise of rising after three days.

The New Testament carries the passage forward in several directions. All three Synoptic Gospels have the confession, and Matthew adds Jesus' blessing of Peter, Matthew 16:18, while Luke repeats the call to take up the cross daily, Luke 9:23. John records a different confession, John 6:68-69. Paul takes up the idea that a believer shares the death of Christ, I have been crucified with Christ, Galatians 2:20, and Peter writes that Christ left an example that we should follow in His footsteps, 1 Peter 2:21, a letter written by the man who in Mark 8 could not accept a suffering Christ. The prediction of glory is picked up in the transfiguration, which Peter later recalls as an eyewitness, 2 Peter 1:16-18, and in the promise that the Son of Man will be seen coming with power, Mark 13:26 and Mark 14:62.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wanted his readers to see that confessing Jesus as the Christ is only the beginning of understanding Him. His first readers believed Jesus was the Christ, and they were facing the question of what that meant for people who were being hauled before courts and exposed to shame. The passage tells them that the confession and the cross belong together. A Christ without a cross is not the Christ Jesus is.

He also meant to show how easy it is to hold a true belief with a false idea attached. Peter says the right word and has the wrong picture, and Mark gives no sign that Peter is being insincere. His rebuke in verse 32 comes out of love and loyalty. That is why Jesus' reply is so sharp, because the danger comes from a friend who speaks reasonably.

Third, Mark meant the call in verses 34 to 38 to be heard by every reader, not only the Twelve. Jesus calls the crowd, and the saying is said to all who want to come after Him. The conditions are the same for all. The Gospel is written for a church that must decide whether to be ashamed of Jesus or not, and the warning in verse 38 is addressed to them directly.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative describes Peter's confession and error, and it is not a pattern to copy. Believers are not told to rebuke Jesus or the Scriptures when the cost of discipleship looks too high. The correction applies to every Christian who prefers a comfortable version of faith. What the passage does prescribe is the teaching in verses 34 to 38, which is spoken as instruction to everyone who wants to follow.

Deny yourself and take up your cross is not a call to seek pain, and it does not say that every hardship is a cross. It speaks of the willingness to give up one's own claim to run one's life, and to follow Jesus where it costs, even to the point of dying for Him. In many places the call is literal and in others it is lived out in daily choices, as Luke's addition of daily suggests, Luke 9:23. Reading it as permission for suffering imposed by abuse, or as a command to endure harm from others, would distort it. The cross in the text is what a person takes up for Christ's sake and the gospel's.

The prophecy about the kingdom in 9:1 is a promise about what some will see, and it is not a timetable for the end. Interpreters have understood it in different ways, and nothing in the practice of the church depends on settling the question, but what it assures all hearers is that the kingdom will be seen with power.

debates.question: Why does Jesus call Peter Satan so sharply after such a good confession?

views.label: Peter voices the tempter's agenda
views.case: By urging a crown without a cross, Peter echoes the wilderness temptation to seize glory without suffering; Jesus names the source of that thinking, for it would derail the very mission He came to accomplish.

views.label: A rebuke of merely human thinking
views.case: Peter has in mind the things of men, a Messiah on human terms; Jesus corrects not Peter's love but his category, calling him and all disciples to think God's thoughts about the cross.

debates.bearing: Both readings hold that resisting the cross, however well-meant, opposes God's saving plan; the way of the Christ and of His followers runs through suffering to glory.

debates.question: What did Jesus mean that some standing there would see the kingdom come with power?

views.label: The transfiguration, resurrection, and Pentecost
views.case: Within the lifetime of the hearers, the kingdom broke in with power at the transfiguration that immediately follows, and supremely in Jesus' resurrection and the coming of the Spirit, inaugurating the reign of God.

views.label: The whole complex of Christ's saving triumph
views.case: The saying points to the decisive arrival of God's reign in the death, resurrection, ascension, and Spirit-empowered spread of the gospel, all seen by that generation, rather than to the final return.

debates.bearing: Both readings locate the fulfilment within the hearers' lifetime in the events that established Christ's reign, not in a failed prediction of an immediate end.

study.originalLanguages:
Peter's word, christos, is the Greek translation of the Hebrew mashiach, the anointed one. The word is a verbal adjective that means anointed, and in Mark it works as a title, so that Mark's opening line already calls Jesus the Christ, Mark 1:1. Peter's answer is the shortest of the three Synoptic versions. In Matthew he adds, the Son of the living God, and in Luke, the Christ of God. Mark gives only the title, and then Jesus does something unexpected with it. The charge to say nothing, verse 30, uses the verb epitimao, which means to rebuke or to warn sharply. It is the verb Mark has used for Jesus silencing a demon, Mark 1:25, and for stilling the storm, Mark 4:39. The same word appears twice more in the next three verses, when Peter rebukes Jesus and when Jesus rebukes Peter, so that the passage is framed by a stack of rebukes.

The verb in verse 31 is dei, it is necessary. The Son of Man must suffer. This is the language of divine necessity, not of fate, and it sets the cross inside God's plan. The word for be rejected, apodokimazo, means to reject after examination, to find unfit. It is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses in Psalm 118:22 for the stone the builders rejected, and Mark will quote the psalm in Mark 12:10. The prediction thus already contains the psalm. Mark adds that Jesus said all this parresia, openly or frankly, verse 32, which contrasts with the secret teaching in parables and with the command of silence in verse 30.

Jesus says to Peter, hypage opiso mou, get behind Me, verse 33. The phrase opiso mou, behind Me, is exactly the phrase of the original call in Mark 1:17, come after Me. A disciple is one who walks behind. Peter was in front, trying to lead, and Jesus puts him back in the place of a follower. Satan, the adversary, is the word used for the tempter in the wilderness, Mark 1:13.

Verse 33 sets two mindsets against each other, with the verb phroneo, to think or have in mind. It means more than a passing thought; it is a way of setting the mind, a settled outlook, as in Philippians 2:5. Peter's outlook is that of men and not of God.

The call of verse 34 is made of three imperatives, and their tenses carry weight. Deny, aparnesastho, and take up, arato, are in the aorist, the tense of a decisive act, while follow, akoloutheito, is in the present, the tense of continuing action. A single decisive refusal of self and a single taking up of the cross begin a following that has no end. The verb aparneomai, deny, is the very word that Jesus will use of Peter's denial in the courtyard, Mark 14:30 and 14:72. Peter is being warned that if he will not deny himself he will end up denying his Lord.

The word psyche appears four times in verses 35 to 37, and the BSB translates it as life twice and soul twice. The same word covers both, and the passage plays on it. Gaining the whole world is set against losing the psyche, and nothing can be exchanged for it. The verse is not about a part of the person called a soul, but the whole self, one's life before God.

In 9:1 the clause the kingdom of God arrive with power uses a perfect participle, which describes something that has already come by the time it is seen.

typology.fulfillment: The psalm speaks of a stone the builders rejected that became the cornerstone. In Mark 8:31 Jesus says He will be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, the builders of Israel's religious life, and Mark has him quote the psalm directly in Mark 12:10. The escalation is that the stone is not merely a figure for the nation, as it may have been in the psalm, but a person, and the rejection is the road to His exaltation. Peter, who rebuked the idea, later preaches this very text, Acts 4:11, and writes of the living Stone, 1 Peter 2:4-7. The type falls short only in that it does not tell us how the rejection would be undone, which the resurrection supplies.

Isaiah describes a servant who is despised and rejected, who carries our sorrows and is pierced for our transgressions, Isaiah 53:3-5, and who afterwards is raised and lifted up, Isaiah 52:13. Jesus' prediction has the same pattern of suffering followed by vindication, and the early church read the Gospel through this lens, Acts 8:32-35. The escalation is that the Servant's suffering is now identified with the Son of Man and the Christ, and the death is for others. The correspondence has limits in Mark 8 itself, where the atoning purpose is not yet stated. Mark waits until Mark 10:45 to say that the Son of Man came to give His life as a ransom for many.

Daniel sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receiving everlasting dominion, Daniel 7:13-14. Jesus takes the title for Himself and adds the necessity of suffering, which Daniel's vision did not mention. Verse 38 draws on the vision, and the kingdom promise of 9:1 and the later saying in Mark 14:62 carry it on, where Jesus says the high priest will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds. The escalation is that the figure of glory goes to His throne by way of the cross. The type is not exhausted in the first coming, since the glory of verse 38 still awaits.

typology.type: The tempter's offer of a crown without a cross
typology.fulfillment: In the wilderness the tempter offered Jesus the kingdoms of the world without suffering, a story Mark compresses to a single verse, Mark 1:13. Peter's rebuke is the same offer from a friend's mouth, and Jesus uses the same word, Satan. The correspondence shows that the temptation was not once and done, but returned. Hebrews says He was tempted in every way, yet without sin, Hebrews 4:15. The type falls short in that Peter is not the devil, and Jesus does not say that he is. Jesus says Peter is speaking the devil's mind, and then He calls him back to follow behind.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ by showing what kind of Christ He is. In Mark's Gospel the title is given at the start and withheld from the lips of others until Peter says it here. Even then, Jesus accepts it only to redefine it. The Christ of this passage is the one who must suffer, be rejected after examination and killed, and who will rise after three days. The word must is the language of obedience to the Father, which gives the cross its place in God's plan. Mark 10:45 will give the purpose: He came to give His life as a ransom for many. The passage is the first step toward that sentence.

Second, He leads by His title for Himself. The Son of Man is not a term the disciples have in mind when they speak of the Christ, and Jesus fastens the two together. In Daniel 7:13-14 the Son of Man receives universal and everlasting dominion, and in Isaiah 53 the servant is crushed for iniquities. Jesus puts them in one figure. He is the one who will come with the clouds and the one who goes down first into rejection. Mark leaves the reader no room to choose between the two. In Mark 14:62 He will say to the high priest that he will see the Son of Man coming with the clouds, and the saying comes while He is on trial for His life.

Third, His rebuke of Peter shows His own commitment to the way of the cross. He turns and looks at His disciples before He speaks, verse 33, as if the rebuke were for them all. The same Jesus who was tempted in the wilderness refuses the same temptation again, and He does so in public. Hebrews 12:2 says that for the joy set before Him He endured the cross, scorning its shame. His refusal to be ashamed is the ground of His demand that we not be ashamed of Him.

Fourth, He leads by example. Peter later wrote that Christ suffered for us, leaving an example, 1 Peter 2:21. He does not ask of the disciples what He will not do Himself. Yet He is more than an example. Paul says, I have been crucified with Christ, Galatians 2:20, and that He loved me and gave Himself up for me. The cross He calls us to take up is not the same as His. His cross bears sin, and ours is the shape of following the one who bore it. The two must not be confused.

Fifth, He leads by the promise of glory. Verse 38 pairs the shame of the cross with the glory of the Father and the angels. The One who is despised and rejected is the One who will come in glory. The transfiguration, which follows within a week, will give three of the disciples a glimpse of that glory, Mark 9:2. The cross and the crown are held together in one Lord.

A caution is needed. The passage does not turn every hardship into a type of Christ's suffering, and it does not say that Peter's confession was empty. It says that a true confession can be wrongly understood, and that the cure is to follow the Christ who explains Himself on the way.
study.god:
This passage shows a God whose plan includes suffering, and who holds that plan with a necessity that is not cold. The must of verse 31 does not mean that God is a fate that Jesus cannot escape. It means that the Father's purpose to save runs through the cross, and that the Son goes to it by choice. The doctrine of God that this passage holds is that sovereignty and love are not rivals. God's plan is certain, and it is a plan that costs the Son His life.

The passage shows that God's thoughts are not our thoughts, which is the heart of the rebuke in verse 33. The things of men are what come naturally: self-preservation, glory, a Messiah who wins without bleeding. The things of God are different, and they are good news to those who can receive them. Isaiah had said as much, that God's ways are higher than ours, Isaiah 55:8-9. The mystery of the cross is not that it shows God to be unlike what we expected, but that it shows what He has been like all along, the God who bears with His people.

The passage shows a God who tells the truth about the cost. Jesus does not hide the cross from the crowd, and He does not offer a discount. God's way of calling people is honest. He tells those who would follow what it will cost, and He tells them what it will gain. The warning about shame and the promise of saving the life are given in the same breath.

The passage shows God as Judge and glorious King. The Son of Man will come in the Father's glory with the holy angels, verse 38, and those who were ashamed of Him will find that He is ashamed of them. The Father who is mentioned here is the Father of glory. The picture is serious, and it is meant to steady those who are tempted to hide their faith.

It also shows a God who is patient with His friends. Peter is rebuked and kept. The passage continues without his dismissal, and the story of Peter goes on, through his denial and his restoration, John 21:15-19. The God who corrects hard is the God who does not discard.

For worship, the passage calls us to confess Christ with our lips and to follow Him with our lives. It invites us to praise the One who gave Himself and to pray for the mind of God in place of the mind of men. It also warns against a worship that wants the crown and not the cross.

crossReferences.note: The kings of the earth and the rulers conspire against the LORD and His Anointed One. This is the background of the title Peter uses. The anointed king is opposed by the powers of the world, and Mark's story shows how that opposition comes first from the leaders of Israel.

The servant is despised and rejected, carries our sorrows, is pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities. The prediction of verse 31 uses the same pattern of rejection leading to death. The prophecy also explains why the suffering was not a defeat: by His stripes we are healed.

One like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives dominion, glory and an everlasting kingdom. Jesus' favourite title for Himself comes from this vision, and verse 38 speaks of His coming in glory in the language of Daniel. The suffering that Jesus adds is the new element.

The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The Greek of the psalm uses the same verb for rejected as Mark 8:31. Jesus will quote the verse in Mark 12:10, and Peter will preach it in Acts 4:11. The rejection and the exaltation are joined in a single verse.

Satan tests Jesus in the wilderness for forty days, and Mark gives it in two verses. Peter's rebuke recalls the same temptation to take a shorter road to the kingdom. When Jesus calls Peter Satan, He is naming the same voice that spoke in the desert.

The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many. This is the answer to the question left open in 8:31, why the Christ must suffer. The reader who has followed the three predictions arrives here at the reason.

Luke records the same call with one addition, that the disciple must take up his cross daily. The word daily shows that the call is not a single act of martyrdom but a pattern of life, and it clarifies how the demand of verse 34 reaches ordinary Christians.

Paul says that he has been crucified with Christ, that he no longer lives, and that Christ lives in him. This is the apostolic reading of taking up the cross: the self that wanted to rule is put to death, and a new life by faith takes its place. It shows that the call of Jesus has become the shape of the Christian life.

Peter writes that Christ suffered for us, leaving an example that we might follow in His footsteps. It is striking that the man who rebuked the first prediction ends by teaching it. The letter shows what happened to Peter after Mark 8, and gives hope to those who are slow to learn.

Jesus tells Peter that before the rooster crows twice he will deny Him three times, using the same verb as the call to deny yourself in 8:34. Peter refuses to deny himself and ends by denying his Lord. The link makes the call to self-denial sharper, and prepares for his restoration.

Christ, who existed in the form of God, emptied Himself, became obedient to death on a cross, and was highly exalted. Paul tells the same story as Mark 8: the way to glory goes down through humbling. The hymn explains why the suffering Christ is also the Lord to whom every knee will bow.

Peter recalls that he was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty on the holy mountain, where the voice came from the Majestic Glory. The glory that Jesus promised in 8:38 and 9:1 was seen by Peter within a week, and he treated it as a certain guarantee, not a fable, of the coming of the Lord.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is the story of a promised king and a people who are not sure what kind of king to want. From the first promise of a seed who would crush the serpent, Genesis 3:15, the hope grows. God chooses Abraham, then Judah, then David, and the psalms and prophets speak of an anointed one who will rule the nations. But the same prophets also speak of a servant who is despised and rejected and pierced. For centuries these two lines run side by side, and Israel is slow to see that they belong to one person.

Mark 8 is the moment when the two lines are drawn together. Peter confesses the first, the anointed king, and Jesus at once announces the second, the suffering servant. He joins them in one title, the Son of Man, and gives the combination a reason, must. The story of redemption could not be completed by a king who simply conquered, because the problem was not Rome but sin and death. The Christ must be killed because only a death could deal with them, and He must rise because death cannot hold Him.

The passage also draws the people of God into the story. The call to take up a cross makes discipleship a sharing in the pattern of the Christ's own path, from suffering to glory. The church is a cross-bearing people, as Paul and Peter both say. Their lives are lived in the time between the cross and the coming of the Son of Man in glory, verse 38, and they live it by faith, not by sight.

What it sets up is Jerusalem. The next chapters take Jesus to the transfiguration, which is a preview of the glory, and then to the cross, which is the cost. The resurrection answers verse 31 and opens the way for the kingdom to come with power, as 9:1 promised, at Pentecost and beyond.

The story ends where verse 38 points, with the Son of Man coming in glory and the whole creation brought under His rule. In Revelation the Lamb who was slain is the one who is worthy to open the scroll, Revelation 5:9-10, and the people who follow Him are those who did not love their lives so much as to shrink from death, Revelation 12:11. The losing of life for His sake becomes the saving of it, and the kingdom that arrived in power at the cross and the empty tomb is finally seen by all.

quiz.q: How did Peter answer Jesus' question, who do you say I am?

options.text: You are the Christ, the promised Messiah.
options.note: Mark 8:29; Peter's true and pivotal confession.

options.text: You are a great prophet like Elijah or John.
options.note: That was what others said; Peter went further and confessed Him as the Christ.

options.text: You are the anointed King, though Peter did not yet grasp the suffering it involved.
options.note: Accurate and insightful, but the plain answer Peter gave is You are the Christ.

options.text: You are only a teacher sent from God.
options.note: Peter confessed far more: the Christ, not merely a teacher.

quiz.q: What did Jesus immediately begin to teach after Peter's confession?

options.text: That the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and after three days rise again.
options.note: Mark 8:31; Jesus redefines the Messiah by the cross and resurrection.

options.text: That the Messiah would soon overthrow the Romans.
options.note: The opposite of Jesus' teaching; He spoke of suffering and death, not political conquest.

options.text: That He would suffer and die for the sins of His people.
options.note: True to His mission, but here Mark records specifically the suffering, rejection, death, and rising He foretold.

options.text: That the disciples would rule with Him in glory at once.
options.note: Glory comes, but only through the cross; Jesus first taught His suffering, not immediate rule.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus rebuke Peter as Satan?

options.text: Because Peter, resisting the cross, had in mind the things of men, not the things of God.
options.note: Mark 8:33; opposing the necessary suffering echoed the tempter's agenda.

options.text: Because Peter had spoken a false confession.
options.note: Peter's confession was true; his error was resisting the way of the cross.

options.text: Because Peter tried to spare Jesus from suffering, thinking in human terms.
options.note: Correct in substance, but the sharpest point is that this was the things of men opposing God's plan.

options.text: Because Peter wanted to follow Jesus too closely.
options.note: The issue was not closeness but Peter's human-minded rejection of the cross.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say it means to follow Him?

options.text: To deny oneself, take up one's cross, and follow Him, losing one's life for Him and the gospel to truly save it.
options.note: Mark 8:34-35 gives the cross-shaped call of discipleship.

options.text: To give up some comforts and try to live a good life.
options.note: The call is far more radical: denying self and taking up the cross, not merely giving up comforts.

options.text: To surrender one's own agenda and follow Jesus wholeheartedly.
options.note: True in spirit, but it should include the striking image of taking up the cross and losing one's life for Him.

options.text: To gain as much of the world as possible for God's glory.
options.note: Jesus warns that gaining the world while forfeiting the soul profits nothing.

quiz.q: What warning does Jesus give about being ashamed of Him?

options.text: The Son of Man will be ashamed of that person when He comes in His Father's glory with the holy angels.
options.note: Mark 8:38; present shame of Christ leads to being disowned at His coming.

options.text: Such a person will simply miss out on some blessings.
options.note: The warning is far graver: being disowned by the Son of Man at His glorious coming.

options.text: The person will face Christ's disapproval when He returns in glory.
options.note: Close, but the text specifically says the Son of Man will be ashamed of, that is, disown, them.

options.text: Nothing will come of it, since God forgives everything anyway.
options.note: Jesus issues a real and solemn warning, not a promise that shame carries no consequence.

questions: Jesus asks each person directly, who do you say I am? How would you answer Him honestly today, and does your life match your words?
Peter confessed the Christ rightly yet recoiled from the cross. Where might you be embracing Jesus while resisting the suffering His way involves?
Jesus calls us to deny ourselves and take up the cross. What would self-denial concretely look like for you this week?
Jesus warns that gaining the whole world profits nothing if we forfeit our souls. Where are you tempted to trade what matters most for what matters least?
Jesus speaks of being ashamed of Him in an adulterous generation. In what settings are you tempted to hide your allegiance to Christ, and how might you own Him instead?

translationNotes.note: Must suffer translates a word of divine necessity; the cross is not an accident but the appointed way of the Christ, foretold in Scripture.
Life and soul render the one Greek word psyche; the saying turns on its double sense, physical life and the true self, so that saving the one can mean losing the other.

The kingdom of God arriving with power was seen within that generation in the transfiguration, the resurrection, and Pentecost, the decisive inbreaking of God's reign, not a prediction of the immediate end of the world.
